summary: Defines the Sieve ihave extension, which lets a script use optional Sieve features while still working when those features are missing. It also defines an error command for reporting when no available combination of extensions meets the script's needs. This is a Proposed Standard.

eli5.summary: A recipe can say, if you have a blender, use it; otherwise do something else. This lets mail rules check which tools are available before using them.

questions: how to write portable sieve scripts
what is the sieve ihave extension
subtitle: Lets a Sieve mail filter script use optional extensions only when they are available, and fail cleanly when they are not.

tldr.problem: A Sieve script must list every extension it uses in a require clause, and it errors out if one is missing, even when the script could work without it.
tldr.mechanism: The ihave extension adds an ihave test that succeeds only if all named capabilities are present, plus an error command that ends the script with a message.
tldr.outcome: Scripts can be portable across servers with different extension sets, and can report when nothing available meets their needs.

today: RFC 5463 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It extends the base language in RFC 5228.

sections.title: The Problem With Require
sections.content:
Sieve (RFC 5228) is a language for filtering email at or around final delivery, on either a mail client or a server. It has no user-controlled loops and cannot run external programs, so it suits servers where users may not run arbitrary programs.

A script lists the extensions it needs in its require clause, and an error results if one is unavailable. That is fine most of the time, but sometimes a script could use an extension if present and still work without it, or would prefer one extension but can use another. The ihave extension serves those cases. Its capability string is ihave.
sections.eli5: Normally a mail rule says, I must have these tools, or I refuse to work. Sometimes it would rather just use whatever tools are there.

sections.title: The ihave Test
sections.content:
The usage is ihave <capabilities: string-list>. The argument is like the one to require: names of one or more Sieve extensions or comparators. The test succeeds if all of them are available. If any is unavailable, the test fails and none of the capabilities are enabled.

Unlike most Sieve tests, ihave takes no match or comparator arguments; the match type is always :is and the comparator is always i;octet. The strings must be constant strings in the sense of Sieve variables (RFC 5229), and passing a non-constant string is an error.
sections.eli5: The test asks, do you have all of these tools? If even one is missing, the answer is no and none of them are used.

sections.title: How It Changes the Rules
sections.content:
Normally every extension used must be named in the initial require. With ihave, these rules change:

  • After a successful ihave test, use of that extension is allowed through to the end of the script, even outside the block the test encloses. Using it earlier MUST cause a run-time error.
  • If ihave is in the require clause, scripts MUST either defer extension checking to run time or account for ihave tests at parse time. The RFC notes that full parse-time checking may be very difficult because ihave can appear inside anyof, allof and not.
  • If an extension is both required and tested, it can be used anywhere and the test always returns true.
  • The interpreter MUST short-circuit tests and MUST evaluate left to right.

Implementations MUST NOT allow ihave with extensions that change the Sieve grammar, or that change how script content is interpreted, such as encoded-character or variables. The test MUST fail and the extension MUST NOT be enabled in that case.
sections.eli5: Once the check says yes, you may use the tool for the rest of the recipe. But you cannot sneak a tool in before you checked for it.

sections.title: The error Command
sections.content:
The usage is error <message: string>. It ends script execution with a run-time error. The message SHOULD be included in any generated report about the error. Section 2.10.6 of RFC 5228 describes how run-time errors are handled.

Like all Sieve strings, the message is UTF-8 and can hold non-US-ASCII characters, which must be considered when reporting errors. The command is part of this extension so that scripts using ihave can always rely on it. It is meant for cases where no combination of available extensions satisfies the script.
sections.eli5: If none of the backup plans work, the rule stops and leaves a note explaining why.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
The main risk the RFC names is that a script which fails to run for lack of an extension may fail to block dangerous email. Because ihave can make scripts more portable and general, it may improve overall security. It is essentially a more flexible variant of require and adds no new capabilities to an implementation, though the security considerations of base Sieve and of any extension used still apply.

IANA registered the capability name ihave for this RFC, with the contact address being the Sieve discussion list.
sections.eli5: If a mail rule breaks, it might stop blocking bad mail. Letting rules adapt to what is available helps them keep working.
